front: A 1000 kg car accelerates from 0 to 30 m/s in 6 seconds. What is the average net force?
why: F = ma with a = dv/dt is the core mechanics calculation on every exam

front: A 2 kg ball at 5 m/s has momentum of:
why: p = mv definition; tested every administration

front: A 70 kg adult weighs about {{c1::700 N}}, so each foot carries roughly {{c1::350 N}} in quiet standing.
why: Estimation anchor for body weight; sanity-check trivia, not a tested concept

front: A ball on a string swings in a horizontal circle (conical pendulum). What does each component of tension do?
why: Conical pendulum is a niche setup; component reasoning is covered by tension/circular cards

front: A ball rolls without slipping. What links $v$ and $\omega$, and does static friction do work?
why: Rolling without slipping and v = wr are off the AAMC outline

front: A block hangs from two symmetric ropes. How does rope angle affect tension?
why: Two-rope tension with angle is a classic component problem

front: A book rests on a table. The reaction force to its weight (per the third law) acts on:
why: Applied third-law pair identification; frequently tested trap

front: A cart is released from height $h$ and runs a vertical loop of radius $R$. Which two relations must be combined?
why: Loop-the-loop from a height combines energy and circular motion; secondary to each alone

front: A centrifuge rotor of radius 4 cm spins at 3000 rpm. Roughly how many g does the sample experience?
why: Centrifuge g-force calculation; lab-relevant but a second-step passage item

front: A diver tucks mid-somersault. What is conserved, and what happens to spin rate and rotational kinetic energy?
why: Angular momentum conservation and rotational KE are off the MCAT outline

front: A machine can reduce the required {{c1::force}} but never the required {{c1::work}}.
why: Machines reduce force, never work; the core simple-machine principle

front: A patient carries a heavy suitcase in the right hand. Why does a cane in the LEFT hand reduce right hip joint force?
why: Hip-cane torque application; plausible biomechanics passage, second step

front: A projectile is launched at 30° above the horizontal at 20 m/s. What is the horizontal component of its initial velocity?
why: Projectile velocity component calculation shows up on essentially every exam

front: A uniform beam rests on two supports. Where does its weight act in the torque equation?
why: Beam weight acts at center of mass; needed for standard torque problems

front: An inclined plane's ideal mechanical advantage equals {{c1::incline length divided by height}}.
why: Inclined-plane MA = length/height; simple machines are on the outline

front: At fixed mass and radius, a plot of centripetal force versus $v^2$ is a straight line of slope {{c1::$m/r$}}.
why: Graph-reading of F_c vs v^2; useful data-interpretation skill, secondary

front: Center of mass versus center of gravity: when do they differ?
why: COM vs COG distinction never matters on the MCAT (uniform g assumed)

front: Centripetal acceleration equals {{c1::$v^2/r$}} and always points {{c1::toward the center}}.
why: a_c = v^2/r toward the center; tested every year

front: Centripetal acceleration must carry units of m/s$^2$, so of $v^2/r$ and $v/r^2$ only {{c1::$v^2/r$}} is possible.
why: Dimensional-analysis screening of a_c; units reasoning is tested but restates the v^2/r card

front: Compare static and kinetic friction.
why: f = uN with static > kinetic friction is tested every administration

front: Define torque and when it is maximized.
why: Torque definition and maximization; duplicates the cloze torque card so ranks below it

front: Equilibrium requires:
why: Net force and net torque zero for equilibrium; duplicates the cloze equilibrium card

front: Fixed pulley versus movable pulley: what does each accomplish?
why: Fixed vs movable pulley MA; pulleys are a common discrete

front: For a satellite in circular orbit, what supplies centripetal force and what follows?
why: Orbital speed from gravity as centripetal force; secondary gravitation result

front: For a vector at angle theta from the x-axis, $V_x =$ {{c1::$V\cos\theta$}} and $V_y =$ {{c1::$V\sin\theta$}}.
why: Vector components Vcos/Vsin underlie every force and projectile problem

front: Give centripetal acceleration and force.
why: Centripetal acceleration and force formulas; restates the cloze a_c card

front: Give the components of gravity on an incline of angle $\theta$.
why: mg sin/mg cos incline components are used on essentially every exam

front: Gravitation: {{c1::$F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$}}, where $r$ is measured {{c1::center to center}}.
why: Universal gravitation inverse-square law; on outline, commonly tested

front: How should you choose the pivot point in a static equilibrium problem?
why: Choosing the pivot at an unknown force is the key torque-problem technique

front: If Earth's radius doubled with mass unchanged, what happens to surface g?
why: Inverse-square proportional reasoning for g; common discrete

front: In uniform circular motion, speed is constant but {{c1::velocity and acceleration}} constantly change direction.
why: Uniform circular motion: constant speed, changing velocity and acceleration

front: Is an astronaut orbiting Earth actually weightless?
why: Weightlessness in orbit restates the apparent-weight/free-fall card

front: Is the outward push you feel on a spinning ride a real force?
why: Centrifugal force as fictitious restates the centripetal card's back

front: Kinetic energy equals:
why: KE = 1/2 mv^2 is tested every year

front: List the main kinematic equations.
why: Kinematic equations are the base of every motion calculation

front: Mechanical advantage equals {{c1::$F_{out}/F_{in}$}}; for a lever it equals {{c1::the ratio of lever arms}}.
why: Mechanical advantage definition and lever-arm ratio; core outline content

front: Near a surface gravitational PE is {{c1::$mgh$}}, but at astronomical distances it is {{c1::$-GMm/r$}}.
why: mgh vs -GMm/r; mgh is core, the general form is secondary

front: Newton's third-law pairs always act on {{c1::two different objects}} and are {{c1::equal and opposite}}.
why: Third-law pairs act on different objects; tested every administration

front: On an incline, which weight component drives sliding and which sets the normal force?
why: Incline weight components and normal force; duplicates the components card

front: Over exactly one full revolution, average velocity is {{c1::zero}} while average speed is {{c1::$2\pi r/T$}}.
why: Average velocity vs average speed over a loop; common displacement/distance discrete

front: Relative centrifugal force compares {{c1::$\omega^2 r$}} with {{c1::$g$}}, so it is reported in multiples of gravity.
why: Relative centrifugal force restates the centrifuge g-force card

front: Rising onto tiptoe makes the foot a {{c1::second-class}} lever with the pivot at {{c1::the toes}} and the load at the ankle.
why: Tiptoe as second-class lever; biomechanics example of lever classes

front: Tension in an ideal massless rope over a frictionless pulley is {{c1::the same everywhere}}.
why: Uniform tension in ideal rope is the assumption behind every pulley problem

front: The center of mass of a two-mass system lies {{c1::closer to the heavier mass}}.
why: Center of mass formula and location; on outline, tested regularly

front: The centripetal force does {{c1::zero}} work in uniform circular motion.
why: Centripetal force does zero work; common conceptual question

front: Torque equals {{c1::$rF\sin\theta$}}, with $r$ measured from {{c1::the pivot to the point where the force acts}}.
why: Torque = rF sin(theta) is used on every exam

front: Torque has units of {{c1::N$\cdot$m}}, so of $Fr$, $F/r$, and $Fr^2$ only {{c1::$Fr$}} can be a torque.
why: Torque units and dimensional screening; supporting units skill

front: Torque plotted against the angle between $r$ and $F$ peaks at {{c1::90 degrees}} and falls to zero at {{c1::0 and 180 degrees}}.
why: Torque vs angle sine plot restates the torque definition card

front: Translational equilibrium means {{c1::$\Sigma F = 0$}}; rotational equilibrium means {{c1::$\Sigma \tau = 0$}}.
why: Translational and rotational equilibrium conditions; tested every year

front: True weight is {{c1::$mg$}}, while apparent weight equals {{c1::the normal force}}.
why: Apparent weight = normal force in elevators is a yearly discrete

front: Two objects have equal kinetic energy but different masses. The heavier one has:
why: p = sqrt(2mKE) relation between KE and momentum; common comparison question

front: Two perpendicular vectors of equal magnitude $V$ give a resultant of {{c1::$V\sqrt{2}$}}.
why: Perpendicular vector addition by Pythagoras; frequent quick calculation

front: What are the conditions for full equilibrium?
why: Near-restatement of the equilibrium conditions cards

front: What condition keeps an object from tipping over?
why: Tipping condition from center of mass over base; plausible balance passage item

front: What is terminal velocity?
why: Terminal velocity when drag equals weight; regularly tested

front: What is the minimum speed at the top of a vertical loop to maintain contact?
why: Minimum loop speed sqrt(gr); classic circular-motion problem

front: What sets the maximum speed for a car rounding a flat curve?
why: Max curve speed sqrt(u g r) from friction as centripetal force; classic

front: When may force magnitudes be added directly instead of by components?
why: Generic advice on when to add forces directly

front: Which lever class has the fulcrum in the middle, and which always has MA below 1?
why: Lever classes and MA below 1 for third-class levers; tested in biomechanics

front: Why can molars generate far more bite force than incisors?
why: Jaw lever-arm reasoning for bite force; plausible passage application

front: Why do horizontally launched and dropped objects land together?
why: Independence of horizontal and vertical motion; tested every year

front: Why do muscles insert close to joints if that demands more force?
why: Why muscles insert near joints; speed vs force trade-off in body levers

front: Why does a two-pan balance read the same on the Moon while a spring scale does not?
why: Balance vs spring scale on the Moon is mass/weight trivia

front: Why does friction on the drive tires point forward for an accelerating car?
why: Static friction pushing a car forward; conceptual third-law application

front: Why does lifting a box with a rounded back produce enormous compressive force on the lumbar spine?
why: Lumbar torque during lifting; biomechanics passage application

front: Why does mass distribution change how fast an object rolls down a ramp?
why: Moment of inertia and rolling races are off the MCAT outline

front: Why is a car at constant speed on a circular track not in equilibrium?
why: Constant speed on a circle is not equilibrium; common conceptual trap

front: Why is the biceps force so much larger than the weight held in the hand?
why: Biceps torque balance is the classic body-lever calculation
